斯特羅小提琴常見於早期錄音室，因方向性強、音量大，適合留聲機錄音；也用於小型劇場: The Stroh violin was common in early recording studios, since its strong directionality and high volume suited gramophone recording; it was also used in small theatres and music halls. In the 1920s the tango orchestra leader Julio De Caro played one live in Buenos Aires, where it was known as the "horn violin". Villa-Lobos used it in Uirapuru, and Kagel's "1898" calls for rebuilt Stroh violin, viola, cello and double bass with a boys' choir. Today it also appears in experimental ensembles in New York, on pop tours and on recordings.
斯特羅小提琴是一種以金屬共鳴器與喇叭機械擴音的弦樂器，喇叭接在指板末端，用以向觀: The Stroh violin is a string instrument amplified mechanically by a metal resonator and a horn, the horn being fixed at the end of the fretboard to project the sound towards the audience or into a recording horn, and the player often has a small monitoring horn beside the ear. It belongs to the violin family, and the same conversion has been applied to the viola, cello, double bass, ukulele, mandolin and guitar. It was common in early recording studios, small theatres and music halls; the Buenos Aires tango orchestra leader Julio De Caro also used one in live performance.
斯特羅小提琴由法蘭克福出身的電氣工程師約翰尼斯·馬蒂亞斯·奧古斯塔斯·斯特羅於一: The Stroh violin was created in London in 1899 by Johannes Matthias Augustus Stroh, an electrical engineer from Frankfurt, as a way of amplifying a string instrument mechanically with a metal resonator and a horn. He applied for a British patent in 1899 and was granted it in 1900, and the next year improved the diaphragm with a conical resonator and a corrugated rim. In the late 1920s, when record companies changed to microphone recording, the habit of using the instrument in the studio faded. Julio De Caro used one in tango performance in Buenos Aires, and there are similar designs such as the Prague violin horn and the Romanian horn violin.
斯特羅小提琴音色獨特而富有穿透力，具有明亮、刺激性的音質，帶有輕微的金屬感。其音: The Stroh violin has a distinctive, carrying tone, bright and a little raw, with a slight metallic edge. Its range is the same as an ordinary violin's, but the sound is sharper and stronger. Because a metal resonator disc replaces the wooden body, the sound travels further and decays less. The disc turns the vibration of the strings into a strong, direct sound wave, producing an effect like a horn. Against a traditional violin, the Stroh lacks warmth and restraint, but it stays clear out of doors or in a noisy room. Its tone comes near the brass of jazz, rough and full of rhythm, and it suits jazz, folk and early recording work.
